4 Arctic Council Annual Report 2025

FOREWORD
Reflecting on an eventful year marked by evolving geopolitics and a growing 
global focus on the Arctic, Mathieu Parker, Director of the Arctic Council 
Secretariat, answers three core questions about the Secretariat’s role in 
supporting the Arctic Council.

1) What do you consider as the biggest 
highlight of 2025?

For the Arctic Council Secretariat (ACS), Indigenous 
Peoples’ Secretariat (IPS) and the Arctic Council at 
large, 2025 was defined by a pivotal moment: the tran-
sition of the Chairship from Norway to the Kingdom of 
Denmark in May. The transition was more than a cere-
mony, it was a significant achievement. Through care-
ful drafting, facilitation and sustained engagement, 
the ACS played a critical role during the negotiations 
around the Romssa-Tromsø Statement. In a complex 
geopolitical context, bringing together all eight Arctic 
States and six Permanent Participants around the same 
virtual negotiation table was critical in reaching con-
sensus on what has been regarded by all as a strong 
joint statement which set forth important commit-
ments. The transition also provided an opportunity to 
highlight the Arctic Council’s recent milestones and el-
evate its work, demonstrating to global audiences that 
the Arctic Council is not only just alive, but also very 
much active.

2) How has the ACS adapted to the new 
working realities of the Arctic Council? 
It has been several years now that the Arctic Council 
has operated in an uncertain and complex environ-
ment, and change management has become an integral 
part of our planning and work. We have strengthened 
our role as a neutral convenor and facilitator, ensuring 
dialogue amongst the Arctic Council family can contin-
ue in a constructive and solutions-oriented manner. 
This has required new solutions for dialogue, more 
frequent consultations and careful preparation to sup-
port the consensus-building process. At the same time, 
we have reinforced our strategic advisory function to 
provide continuity, institutional memory and practical 
options to help the Council remain effective as priori-
ties evolve. In terms of Working Group and secretarial 

support, there has been close coordination to ensure 
their project work advances despite operational chal-
lenges. Maintaining momentum at this working level 
has been essential to preserving the Council’s credibil-
ity and impact. Finally, we have strengthened invest-
ment in strategic communications. With heightened 
global attention on the Arctic, it is crucial that we clear-
ly communicate the value and results of the Council’s 
work.

3) What is the ACS’s key focus in the future? 

Despite the highs and lows we have been through over 
several years, the Arctic Council – and the principles 
upon which it was established – still stand strong. The 
achievements made in 2025 are a prime example of 
that. While there have and will always be diverging 
views and priorities among Arctic States, the important 
thing is that despite these unique times, the dialogue 
has been able to continue; and we at the ACS and the 
IPS consider ourselves privileged to be able to continue 
to play this convening and facilitation role. 

Looking ahead, our focus is to continue to work con-
structively with the Kingdom of Denmark’s Chairship 
and the incoming Swedish Chairship to ensure that the 
Arctic Council remains adaptable, relevant and respon-
sive in a rapidly evolving environment, while continu-
ing to provide a trusted platform for cooperation in the 
Arctic. 

Mathieu Parker, 
Director of ACS

OUR MANDATE

The ACS enhances the work of the Arctic Council through 
its administrative capacity and by providing continuity, 
institutional memory, operational efficiency, enhanced 
communication and outreach, exchange of information 
with other relevant international organizations and 
support for activities of the Arctic Council.

OUR KEY FUNCTIONS

1. Administrative and organizational support 
The main tasks of the ACS are to support the Chairship in the daily operations of the Arctic Council, 
and to maintain the Council’s legacy, procedures and practices. 

2. Working Group secretarial support 
Arctic Contaminants Action Program (ACAP) and Emergency Prevention, Preparedness and 
Response (EPPR) secretariats are part of the ACS functions. The ACS also provides secretarial 
support for the Expert Group on Black Carbon and Methane (EGBCM), as well as assists other 
subsidiary bodies as resources allow and demand arises. 

3. Communications and outreach 
The ACS coordinates the overall external and internal communications on behalf of the Arctic 
Council, including sharing the important work of the Council with target audiences across the 
Arctic and beyond. 

4. Finance and human resources 
The ACS recruits staff and ensures staff members’ welfare and further development, enhances 
the Council’s IT security, manages the Council’s archives to provide institutional memory and 
continuity, and oversees its budget.

ADMINISTRATIVE AND 
ORGANIZATIONAL SUPPORT 
Since its inception in 2013, there has never been a lack 
of work or interesting changes to contend with at the 
ACS; and 2025 was definitely in keeping with this tra-
dition. Once again, the year included several highlights 
and noteworthy moments: from the first-ever Arctic 
Youth Conference and Arctic Emergency Management 
Conference hosted by the Norwegian Chairship in ear-
ly 2025; to the highly successful 14th Meeting of the 
Arctic Council that saw the transition of the Chairship 
from Norway to the Kingdom of Denmark and the ap-
proval of a critical Romssa-Tromsø Joint Statement; to 
the introduction of innovative new approaches to con-
sultation and convening of the Arctic Council family by 
the Kingdom over the course of its first few months in 
the Chair seat. 

The Chairship Support Team played a key support, ad-
visory, planning and coordination role in all of these 
efforts, ensuring that both the outgoing and incoming 
Chairs were properly supported in implementing the 
priorities and commitments that were agreed to by all 
Arctic States and Permanent Participants. 

Priorities 

Transition coordination and support to the outgo-
ing and incomings Chairs: Throughout the first half 
of 2025, the ACS worked closely with both the outgo-
ing Chairship of Norway and the incoming Chairship 
of the Kingdom of Denmark to ensure the successful 
unfolding of the 14th meeting of the Arctic Council in 
May 2025. The ACS worked closely with Norway in 
supporting the high-level negotiations surrounding the 
approval of the Romssa-Tromsø Joint Statement, the lo-
gistical preparations for the meeting itself, and the de-
velopment of all other transition documents. The ACS 
also met regularly with colleagues from Greenland, 
the Faroe Islands and Denmark to facilitate their tran-
sition into the Chairship role, exchange institutional 
knowledge and support preparations for the upcoming 
Chairship and other Arctic Council matters.

Supporting the implementation of the Romssa-
Tromsø Statement priorities and commitments, 
and the Chairship Program: Although not an official 
priority from an ACS Workplan perspective, the push 
for a continued ramp-up of AC operations was again 
at the forefront of all of our efforts over the course of 
2025, as the ACS worked in lockstep with both Norway 
and the Kingdom of Denmark to: 

• Provide impartial advice, support and guidance 
to the SAO Chair on all matters relating to the 
Chairship transition and the subsequent im-
plementation of the new joint statement and 

Chairship program. 

• Support the preparation, coordination and execu-
tion of all Arctic Council and Chairship meetings, 
including SAO level consultations, and Norwegian 
Chairship meetings with the Council’s Permanent 
Participants, Working Groups/EGBCM and 
Observers.   

• Coordinate consultations, information sharing 
and engagement with subsidiary bodies, Observer 
states and organizations, and other external ac-
tors, both in Tromsø and via different internation-
al fora. 

• Supporting and coordinate Council-wide informal 
groups mandated to develop recommendations 
for SAOs and PPs, notably the Informal Group on 
the Future of Arctic Council Project Financing and 
the Project Support Instrument (PSI), as well as the 
Subcommittee on Strengthening the Sustainable 
Development Working Group (SDWG).

Support for youth engagement, wildland fires and 
other Arctic Council priorities: the ACS supported 
both specific Chairship signature initiatives and broad-
er objectives under the Arctic Council Strategic Plan. 

• On youth engagement, the ACS delivered the 
Chairship Deliverable on Assessing Youth 
Engagement in the Arctic Council, which is the first 
comprehensive assessment of Arctic Council youth 
initiatives in the Council since its inception. The re-
port mapped existing efforts, identified structural 
gaps and put forward concrete recommendations 
for SAOs and PPs to strengthen the Council’s ability 
to engage Arctic youth in a more systematic way. 
In parallel, the ACS maintained its support to the 
Chairship Youth Committee, culminating in its as-
sistance with the overall planning and delivery of 
the Arctic Youth Conference in January 2025. 

• The ACS also provided substantive support to the 
Norwegian Chairship’s Wildland Fires Initiative. 
This work culminated in the 2025 WFI Summary 
Report by the Co-Leads and transitioned into 
follow-on work through the newly established 
Informal Group on Wildland Fires, which com-
menced its activities in the fall with continued ACS 
support.  

Direct engagement and representation with ex-
ternal stakeholders: Beyond its support to SAO Chair 
activities, the ACS served as the central point for the 38 
Observers, collecting reports, answering enquiries, en-
suring communication on the status of work resump-
tion, and hosting several external stakeholders.

Key achievements 
 
Approval of the Romssa-Tromsø Joint Statement 
The ACS played a critical role in the drafting and fa-
cilitation of negotiations towards securing consensus 
around this critical document that set out ambitious 
new priorities and commitments for the Council over 
the next two years despite a challenging geopolitical 
context. Equally important, this new statement offi-
cially welcomed new Work Plans for 2026-2027 for 
each of the Arctic Council’s Working Groups, and also 
approved a new ACS Workplan for this same period. 

Delivering the first Arctic Youth Conference 
and initiating a new youth engagement process 
through the KoD Chairship 
In 2025, the ACS, in close cooperation with IPS, suc-
cessfully delivered the Arctic Youth Conference (AYC) 
in Tromsø under the Norwegian Chairship. The con-
ference brought together contributions from Arctic 
States, Permanent Participants, Working Groups, 
Observers and external organizations, creating 
an inclusive and high-level platform for youth dia-
logue across the circumpolar region. The Norwegian 
Chairship Youth Committee’s work was formally 
concluded with the presentation of its recommen-
dations to the incoming Chairship of the Kingdom of 
Denmark in Copenhagen in June. Building on this mo-
mentum, a new and strengthened Youth Committee 
was established under the Kingdom’s Chairship, with 

a successful in-person launch in Iceland during the 
Arctic Circle Assembly in October. With this renewed 
structure in place, preparations are already well un-
derway to deliver the next Arctic Youth Conference 
in Nuuk in 2027. 

Playing a key convening role for the Arctic Council 
family 
Building on the momentum of the Norwegian 
Chairship, the ACS continued to support Norway 
and the Kingdom of Denmark in exploring new 
ways of engaging with key stakeholders; while also 
helping the broader Arctic Council family connect. 
Throughout this process, the ACS worked in close 
collaboration with the Chairship teams, providing 
advice on various options and helping to facilitate 
these efforts.

The ACAP and EPPR Executive Secretaries continued to

within the Working Groups and the Council, support-
ing the coordination of Norwegian and later Kingdom

and continuing to enable Working Group processes ac-
cording to the agreed-on procedures.

Priorities 
Support to the Working Group Chairs: Supporting 
the Working Group Chairs in organizing online 
Working Group meetings and communication and 
outreach events; providing reports to the SAOs and 
Permanent Participant Heads of Delegation in accor-
dance with the Council’s requirements and as request-
ed; developing background documents; fostering re-
lationships with other subsidiary bodies of the Arctic 
Council and external partners. 

Facilitating Working Group processes: Facilitating 
a functioning decision-making process at the Working 
Group level both through the written procedure and 
online Working Group meetings, in line with the 
Guidelines, the Arctic Council Rules of Procedure and

collecting, consolidating and managing feedback on 
internal reports, deliverables, new project propos-

on any developments and results of the approval 
processes. 

Preparing for the 14th Meeting of the Arctic 
Council: The Secretaries supported project leads / 
Expert Groups in successful and timely finalization of 
products to be considered as deliverables for the 14th 
meeting of the Arctic Council; planned and carried out 
essential Working Group processes with their respec-

new Work Plans and other materials for the Chairship 
transition.

ARCTIC CONTAMINANTS ACTION
PROGRAM (ACAP)

In 2025, the ACAP Executive Secretary provided sup-
port for two ACAP Plenary meetings, two ACAP Heads 
of Delegation meetings (18-19 February & 8-9 October), 
as well as several Expert Group meetings (online for-
mat). During 2025, tasks and responsibilities remained 
largely consistent with those of previous years and 
included ensuring ACAP’s operational efficiency, sup-
porting the work of the ACAP Chair and Expert Groups, 
assisting with planning and reporting processes, meet-
ing and event coordination, facilitating internal and 
external communications, maintaining institutional 
memory and reference materials. Particular emphasis 
was placed on facilitating and strengthening ACAP’s 
communication and outreach activities. 

Key achievements 

Supporting the ACAP Chair and Expert Group 
Chairs in intersessional work and meeting ar-
rangements Throughout 2025, ACAP Executive 
Secretary supported intersessional coordination, fol-
low-up on agreed decisions and tasks, meeting plan-
ning and organization (including documentation), and 
the onboarding of new ACAP and Expert Group mem-
bers. In addition to routine intersessional support, this 
year included the organization of a hybrid AFFF proj-
ect workshop, which took place on 3-5 June, 2025, in 
Helsinki, Finland. 

Contribution to the Chairship’s initiatives xxxxx-xxxxx-
In collaboration with the Arctic Monitoring and 
Assessment Programme and Conservation of Arctic 
Flora and Fauna Secretariats, ACAP Secretariat orga-
nized a side-event on Community-Based Monitoring 
in the Arctic at the Arctic Youth Conference (January 
25, 2025). The Executive Secretary has also provid-
ed support to the ACS in facilitating the Kingdom of 
Denmark’s initiatives. 

Strengthening of ACAP’s Communication and 
Outreach 
Two ACAP projects – Solid Waste Management in 
Remote Arctic Communities and Phase-out of PFAS-
containing Fire-Fighting Foam (AFFF) in the Arctic – 
were featured in the Arctic Council’s biennial Pathways 
magazine. In October 2025, ACAP Secretariat launched 
an ACAP Instagram account. A session proposal “Small 
Investments – Big Changes” developed by the ACAP 
Secretariat in consultation with ACAP Expert Groups 
was accepted for the 2025 Arctic Circle Assembly 
and was delivered as an official session during the 
event, with participation from project leads or their 
representatives.

Arctic Council Annual Report 2025 14

EMERGENCY PREVENTION 
PREPAREDNESS AND RESPONSE 
(EPPR )

In 2025, the core priorities and work for the EPPR 
Executive Secretary remained the same as during the 
previous year, while many processes also continued 
from 2024 until the end of the Norwegian Chairship of 
both the Council and EPPR. Key tasks included secretar-
iat administration, support for processes and projects 
as well as coordination, outreach and representation. 
In addition, 2025 included facilitation and prepara-
tion of transition of the EPPR Chairship from Norway 
to the U.S. as well as new Expert Group Chairs. EPPR 
Executive Group, consisting of the Chairs of the WG 
and the Executive Secretary, met bi-monthly both un-
der the Norwegian and the U.S. Chairships of EPPR, to 
manage and steer the Working Group’s work. 

During the first half of 2025, the Arctic Emergency 
Management Conference organized as a part of the 
Norwegian Chairship of the Arctic Council took a lot of 
focus, including planning, administrative coordination, 
and eventually executing the event, followed up with 
reporting and concluding the process. In addition to 
EPPR work, the Executive Secretary also took part in 
ongoing internal administrative ACS initiatives as well 
as supported ACS and IPS colleagues in facilitating the 
Kingdom of Denmark’s Informal Group on Wildland 
Fires. 

Key achievements

Arctic Emergency Management Conference 
(AEMC) 
EPPR Chair and Executive Secretary, with the guidance 
by the Norwegian Arctic Council Chairship, led the 
planning and organization of the first-of-its-kind 
multidisciplinary conference focusing on EPPR thematic 
areas. The AEMC gathered over 300 participants and 
had over 50 sessions and two workshops in its three-
day program. Support by the ACS Senior PR and Project 
Officers, among other colleagues, helped to carry out 
the conference as planned. 
 

Communication and outreach activities 
EPPR concluded a few hallmark projects in 2024-2025, 
so communication and PR activities on project deliv-
erables with project leads and partners were high on 
the agenda. As usual, the Executive Secretary assisted 
the Chair in planning and drafting speaking points and 
presentations, and coordinated EPPR representation at 
relevant events, to facilitate information sharing and 
external connections. EPPR also launched a new out-
reach platform with a LinkedIn profile in 2025 to better 
reach relevant audiences.

15 Arctic Council Annual Report 2025

COMMUNICATIONS 
In 2025, the ACS scaled up and strengthened the 
Council’s external communications at a time of height-
ened global attention and speculation about the sta-
tus of the Arctic Council. Working closely with both 
the outgoing Norwegian Chairship and the incoming 
Kingdom of Denmark Chairship, the communications 
team played a central role in ensuring a visible, coher-
ent and forward-looking transition in May. A key focus 
was supporting priority themes under the Norwegian 
Chairship, including the Wildland Fire Initiative and 
a communications campaign about the cryosphere, 
and highlighting major milestones and outcomes of 
the outgoing Chairship in the biennial Pathways mag-
azine. Communications efforts also focused on elevat-
ing the Kingdom of Denmark Chairship’s key priorities 
through Arctic Council channels, as well as at interna-
tional conferences and other external forums. 

Given lingering speculation about the Council’s sta-
tus following the 2022 pause in official Arctic Council 
meetings, a substantial focus was dedicated to strength-
ening the Council’s public narrative. The communica-
tions team developed clear, evidence-based messaging 
to demonstrate the Council’s continued activity, im-
pact and importance. This messaging was reflected in 
speeches, media engagements, digital content, social 
media, event materials and other formats. The commu-
nications team produced a significant amount of new 
content, including 61 news and feature articles, and in-
troduced new communication channels and formats to 
elevate the Arctic Council’s work. Close collaboration 
with the Chairship teams, Working Groups and the 
Permanent Participants ensured accuracy, inclusivity 
and strategic alignment. 

Priorities 
 

Social media and content development: The 
Council’s website and social media channels contin-
ued to play a central role in delivering timely, relevant 
information on the Council’s initiatives and projects. 
The ACS prioritized developing engaging content to 
inform diverse audiences and promote Arctic literacy. 
Outreach was expanded with new formats, including 
the launch of the Arctic Council’s first podcast, This 
Way Up. 

Chairship communications support: Over the past 
year, the ACS has worked closely with the Norwegian 
Chairship to amplify messaging related to their priori-
ties, including outreach efforts on topics such as wild-
land fires, the cryosphere, youth engagement and gen-
der. Particular focus was given to wildland fires, where 
the communications team produced videos and a 

podcast episode, organized conference panels and de-
veloped a storymap in partnership with GRID Arendal, 
which published in 2025. In addition, the ACS sup-
ported the incoming Kingdom of Denmark Chairship 
in highlighting their priorities. Moreover, the commu-
nication team provided speaking points for the SAO 
Chair for external speaking engagements and provided 
guidance on media interactions, ensuring strong lead-
ership, consistency and clarity for external audiences. 

Events and outreach planning: External events play 
an important role in highlighting the Council’s work 
and advancements. The ACS devoted significant effort 
planning and executing the Arctic Council’s presence 
at various conferences, including side events at Arctic 
Frontiers, UN Ocean Conference and the Arctic Circle 
Assembly. Moreover, the ACS played a key role in fa-
cilitating the Norwegian Chairship’s events, including 
the Arctic Emergency Management Conference in 
Bodø and the Arctic Youth Conference in Tromsø. The 
communications team also assisted with outreach for 
the Kingdom of Denmark’s Chairship program launch 
event and a special event hosted by the Kingdom of 
Denmark Chairship aboard the Statsraad Lehmkuhl 
in Nuuk and began preparations for the Ocean 
Connectivity Conference in Tórshavn in May 2026. 

Media relations and targeted outreach: Serving as 
the first point of contact for media requests, the ACS 
provided timely responses in coordination with the 
Chairship and relevant Working Groups. The commu-
nication unit also engaged in targeted media outreach, 
including for the 14th meeting in May 2025. To pro-
mote the Arctic Council podcast, the ACS collaborated 
with the newsroom High North News to reach a broad 
audience interested in Arctic issues.

Media monitoring: An essential tool for evaluating 
communications efforts, media monitoring allows the 
ACS to gauge general sentiments towards the Arctic 
Council in news articles, counter misinformation when 
feasible and keep on top of relevant and timely com-
munications opportunities based on the news cycle.

Key achievements
Launch of the Arctic Council podcast This Way 
Up 
In partnership with the IPS, the communications 
team researched, developed, wrote, produced, served 
as hosts and marketed the first three episodes of the 
podcast, which aired in 2025. The podcast, which was 
developed with input from Permanent Participants 
and Working Groups, features prominent experts and 
Knowledge Holders and delves into complex Arctic 
issues by examining specific cases that connects local 
realities to global implications – showing how interna-
tional collaboration plays a crucial role. 

The 14th meeting 
The transition from the Norwegian to the Kingdom of 
Denmark Chairship was an opportunity to highlight 
achievements made during the Norwegian Chairship, 
as well as showcase the importance of continued coop-
eration. The communication team led communications 
and outreach around this event, including organizing 
and facilitating the press conference, writing press re-
leases, conducting media outreach, producing content 

for the website and social channels and preparing 
briefing materials and speaking points for delegates. 

Pathways Magazine 
The communications team produced the biennial mag-
azine Pathways, showcasing the work and achieve-
ments of the Arctic Council for a general audience. 
The 2025 edition featured 39 unique articles and was 
a collaborative effort, including contributions from 
Permanent Participants and Working Groups. The 
communications team led the editorial board, coordi-
nated submissions and oversaw the visual branding 
for the magazine, as well as took a lead in researching, 
interviewing experts, writing articles and editing the 
full magazine.

17 Arctic Council Annual Report 2025

FINANCE AND HUMAN 
RESOURCES 

Despite some uncertainty in terms of financial con-
tributions and some further turnover within the core 
administrative team, the ACS was able to make signifi-
cant progress in a number of identified areas over the 
course of 2025. Consolidating and further strengthen-
ing of the administrative team will be a priority going 
forward. 

Priorities 

Financial Stewardship: Following a 2025 fiscal year 
that saw unexpected staffing changes within the ACS, 
and despite some uncertainty with budgets and con-
tributions, the ACS delivered a result close to target of 
NOK 665 061, demonstrating strong financial account-
ability and a measured risk management approach. 

The audit for 2025 concluded that “the financial state-
ments give a true and fair view of the financial posi-
tion of the Company as at 31 December 2025 and its fi-
nancial performance for the year ended in accordance 
with the Norwegian Accounting Act and accounting 
standards and practices generally accepted in Norway.”

The ACS has continued to develop good financial rou-
tines in close collaboration with the external accoun-
tant (Azets). In addition, increased attention on the 
development of processes and internal controls for 
handling of external project funding has been a key 
focus area over this last year.

People Management: A number of staff chang-
es took place in 2025. For the ACS, Pernille Haukås 
(Norway) started as Intern 16 January 2025. André 
Skrivervik (Norway) started in his position as Head 
of Administration on 1 May. Head of Communications 
Kristina Bär (Sweden) left and was replaced by Anja 
Salo (Norway) who started on 4 August. For the IPS, 
Executive Secretary Anna Degteva (Russia) left after her 
second term contract was concluded. She was replaced 
by Rosa-Máren Magga (Finland) on 1 September. Rosa-
Máren Magga was in turn replaced by Linda Lyberth 
Kristiansen (Greenland) as the new IPS Advisor effec-
tive from 20 September. 

Key Achievements 

Archive review process 
In line with the work plan, the ACS launched an in-
ternal review process of archiving routines and sys-
tems. A project group was formed and started its work 
during the fall. This work continues in 2026 with the 
aim of producing a set of recommendations for a way 
forward. Expected outcomes include a review of exist-
ing guidelines, assessment of technical solutions and 
requirements, and a proposal for a revised filing struc-
ture and naming scheme for storage of documents. 

Routines, processes and templates 
In 2025, an effort has been made to further develop 
internal HR processes, routines and practices. New 
templates have been developed, and an increased fo-
cus has been dedicated to formalization of HR and HSE 
processes, i.e. on/offboarding processes, probation- and 
appraisal conversations to mention a few. 

Staffing 
In addition to the employees mentioned under “People 
management”, the ACS launched two more recruitment 
processes in 2025. One was the reintroduction of the 
role as Web and Digital Media Officer and the second 
was a new intern for 2026. The ACS signed a contract 
with Alex Carlson (U.S.) who will take up his position 
as Web and Digital Media Officer on 20 April 2026. The 
ACS also signed a contract with Malva Hasselstrand 
(Sweden) after having reviewed 315 applications 
for the internship. Hasselstrand will replace Pernille 
Haukås from 1 March 2026. Beyond this, the ACS also 
played a key role in facilitating reengagement between 
the Norwegian MFA and Ministry of Finance on the 
rights and privileges of ACS staff as defined in the Host 
Country Agreement, in particular as it relates to tax 
status and use of D-numbers. The ACS looks forward 
to continued discussions with the MFA and Ministry of 
Finance over the course of 2025, with a view to amend-
ing the HCA in order to address these last outstanding 
recommendations from the 2019 INAO review.

INDIGENOUS PEOPLES’ 
SECRETARIAT 
The Indigenous Peoples’ Secretariat (IPS) was estab-
lished in 1994 to support the Indigenous Peoples’ 
Organizations under the Arctic Environmental 
Protection Strategy. In 1996, the Ottawa Declaration 
recognized the IPS institution and mandated it to work 
under the framework of the Arctic Council. The main 
mandate of the IPS is to facilitate active participation 
and full consultation of all six Permanent Participants 
in the Arctic Council. The IPS has diverse functions 
ranging from assisting with communications among 
the Permanent Participants (PPs) and between PPs and 
the Arctic Council related bodies, to helping with meet-
ing logistics and supporting PPs’ actions on promoting 
environmental protection and the sustainable develop-
ment of Indigenous Peoples’ cultures in the Arctic. 

Priorities and Key achievements 
In 2025, the IPS successfully continued its main man-
date to support PPs’ work in the Arctic Council, with the 
focus on the Council’s Chairship transition process and 
the Norwegian Chairship’s (2023-2025) and Kingdom 
of Denmark’s Chairship (2025-2027) processes to con-
tinue communications and cooperation with all six 
PPs. The IPS remained committed to follow up the 
priorities identified in the IPS work plan: Indigenous 
youth engagement; Arctic Indigenous languages; and 
Arctic Indigenous Peoples’ cooperation. According to 
these priorities, some of the big achievements in 2025 
are:

Facilitating PPs participation in the 14th meet-
ing of the Arctic Council and the transition of 
the Arctic Council Chairship from Norway to 
Kingdom of Denmark: The IPS was instrumental 
in supporting all six Permanent Participants partic-
ipation in processes leading up to the Arctic Council 
Chairship transition and the 14th meeting of the Arctic 
Council. The IPS ensured that PPs input are included 
in the process in advance of the meeting. This includ-
ed maintaining regular communication with both the 
outgoing and the incoming Chairship teams, facilitat-
ing PPs contribution and inclusion in the transition 
process following PPs priorities. IPS helped with the 
translation as well as other logistical and adminis-
trational support for the transition of the Chairship. 
The IPS had a major role in facilitating the consulta-
tion meetings between the Arctic Council Chairship 
(both Norway and Kingdom of Denmark) and the PPs. 
The IPS supported the fourth meeting between the 
Norwegian Chairship, PP and Working Groups (WG) 
in January as well as consultation meetings between 
the Kingdom of Denmark’s Chairship, PP and WG in 
June and Chairship-PP consultation in October. The IPS 

prepared documents, coordinated logistics, facilitated 
communication among participants, and supported ef-
fective participation of PP and PP youth. 

Supporting Permanent Participants’ engagement 
in the Working Groups: Throughout the report-
ing period, IPS provided targeted support to Working 
Groups with facilitating communication between PPs 
and Arctic Council subsidiary bodies and processes. 
The IPS helped some of the WGs with their plenary 
meetings providing back-end technical support and as-
sisting with information exchange, logistics, and coor-
dination with all six PPs. The IPS also served as an on-
going communication bridge between the PPs and the 
Working Groups. IPS continued meetings with Working 
Group Secretariats and participate in webinars rele-
vant to Indigenous Peoples. IPS also helped with the 
translation for the meetings of the Informal Group of 
Wildland fires and helped with the PPs’ participation 
as well as other administrative support needed. 

Strengthening Indigenous youth engagement: In 
2025, one of the main focus areas in IPS’s work was 
to continue supporting Indigenous youth engagement 
and capacity-building to enhance capacity of PPs and 
their youth. The IPS facilitated PP Youth Network and 
helped them to meet regularly. The IPS played an ac-
tive role in planning and implementing the Norwegian 
Chairship’s Arctic Youth Conference (AYC), held in 
January in Tromsø, by contributing to logistics, pro-
gram development, funding of travel support, coordi-
nating PP and PP youth inclusion in planning and par-
ticipation in the conference, to make sure Indigenous 
perspectives are visible. IPS also assisted with World 
Reindeer Herder’s participation in the Conference 
with their NOMAD Indigenous FoodLab. The IPS fa-
cilitated PP Youth participation and preparation in 
One Ocean II expedition in August, chartered by the 
UiT Arctic University of Norway. IPS Advisor attended 
the Expedition as a mentor and supported Indigenous 
youth participation, nominated by the PPs as well as 
ensured that Indigenous perspectives are engaged. As 
a continued practice, the IPS assisted PP Youth partici-
pation in Chairship meetings and other processes. 

Promoting Indigenous Peoples’ work related to 
Wildland Fires: One of the most prominent themat-
ical focus in 2025 for the IPS was the wildland fire 
work, first under the Norwegian Chairship’s Wildland 
Fire Initiative (WFI) and processes continuing to the 
Kingdom of Denmark’s Chairship by ensuring PP and 
Indigenous Knowledge holders’ engagement. The 
IPS assisted with meeting facilitation and transla-
tions whenever needed. IPS supported PPs participa-
tion in planning of the Norwegian Chairship’s Arctic 
Emergency Management Conference in March, by con-
tributing to the conference report and a Sharing Circle 
on Emergency Management in the Arctic. The IPS also

livelihoods and issues. The IPS was instrumental in en-

communications products. These include Pathways 
magazine and ‘This Way Up’ Arctic Council podcast 
that IPS co-creates and co-hosts. The IPS ensured that 
PPs voice, knowledge and input was included in the 
products.
